clue.text: Well turned-out poet

Christopher ..., the 18th-century English poet of Jubilate Agno

explanation.definitionFit: Someone well turned-out is elegantly dressed, and Christopher Smart was an eighteenth-century English poet.

clue.text: Galsworthy prop a disappointment to the Prince of Aragon

explanation.surface: A stage object from a Galsworthy play is likened to the Prince of Aragon's letdown.
explanation.definitionFit: Galsworthy's 1906 play centres on a stolen silver cigarette case, and Aragon loses Portia by choosing the silver casket.

clue.text: Novel missile, variously black and gold ()

definitions.text: Novel missile, variously black and gold

parts.words: Novel missile, variously black and gold
parts.note: a missile shot from a bow that names two novels, Stevenson's black one and Conrad's one of gold

explanation.surface: A projectile from fiction, painted in two colours.
explanation.walkthrough: Stevenson wrote The Black Arrow and Conrad wrote The Arrow of Gold, so this missile appears in both titles, with a different colour each time.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowman's missile that gives its name to Stevenson's The Black Arrow and Conrad's The Arrow of Gold.

clue.text: Italian river is including a lake

explanation.surface: An Italian river is said to contain a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lake' looks like a single definition, but the 'a' is the letter that goes inside; Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee's other name.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, the freshwater lake in northern Israel.

explanation.walkthrough: 6 is 6-down, Damon Runyon; Robert Benchley was an American comic writer. 'put out' rearranges MUIRSHOST.
explanation.definitionFit: Damon Runyon and Robert Benchley were both American comic writers, known for funny stories and essays.

clue.text: US writer starting some terribly exciting innovations now ()

clue.text: Somewhat prejudiced opponent of King John? (45)

explanation.surface: A rather bigoted enemy of England's King John.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's King John the lords Salisbury, Pembroke and Bigot desert the king; the last name also means an intolerant person, the 'prejudiced' joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Bigot is one of the nobles who rebel against the king in Shakespeare's King John.

clue.text: "Why does your brand sae drop wi blude,/-—," (Scots ballad)

definitions.text: Why does your brand sae drop wi blude

parts.words: Why does your brand sae drop wi blude
parts.note: the opening line of a Scots ballad, addressed by a mother to her son, whose name fills the gap

explanation.surface: A line from a Scots ballad asks why a sword drips with blood.
explanation.walkthrough: The traditional Scots ballad opens 'Why dois your brand sae drap wi bluid, Edward, Edward', so the gap is the son's name, repeated as the ballad's title. 'Brand' is an old word for sword.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the son questioned in the Scots ballad of that title, who has killed his father.

clue.text: Detest child, like Shakespeare's executioner

explanation.surface: Hating a child like Shakespeare's hangman would.
explanation.definitionFit: Abhorson is the executioner in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure.

clue.text: Enduring Wilde character

parts.note: a figure in Oscar Wilde's only novel who stays young while his portrait ages

explanation.surface: A lasting creation of Oscar Wilde.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enduring' looks like praise for a classic, but this character literally endures: he never ages while his portrait does.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's hero keeps his youthful looks for decades while his painted portrait grows old and corrupt.

clue.text: Part of a circus type announced in gondolier's song

explanation.walkthrough: A barker is a showman who calls out to attract customers at a circus or fair; 'barker role' spoken sounds like the song.
explanation.definitionFit: A barcarolle is a Venetian boat song, traditionally sung by gondoliers.

clue.text: Exalted description of Liszt work

definitions.meaning: ecstatic, full of extravagant enthusiasm
Liszt composed the Hungarian Rhapsodies, so this adjective describes them

explanation.surface: An elevated description of a piece by Liszt.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means ecstatically enthusiastic, and it also describes Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsodies.

clue.text: It'll fade terribly, like Hopkins's Deutschland

explanation.surface: It will fade badly, like the ship in Hopkins's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerard Manley Hopkins wrote The Wreck of the Deutschland, about a ship lost in 1875.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopkins's poem mourns the wreck of the steamship Deutschland, a doomed vessel lost with many lives.

clue.text: "They keep themselves so thin, they look like pictures " (Tom Wolfe)

definitions.text: They keep themselves so thin, they look like pictures

clue.text: Natural aristocrat in smaller role
